1:
When this happened is disputed by five voices, the question being whether the chapter stands in its own order. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) argues hardest for displacement, holding with the best interpreters that these things were done long before Absalom’s rebellion: Saul’s sin would not have lain unpunished so long, nor the bones of Saul and Jonathan gone unmoved, and David in old age attempting a giant, or his people suffering him to, is improbable. They stand here, he says, because David’s sin being once related it was convenient that his punishments should immediately succeed, which is frequent in scripture-story. John Gill (reformed) reports that view with its grounds but leaves it open, noting that one Jewish writing dates this to the year after Saul was slain while other copies of the same book say thirty years after, and that Abarbinel and some of the best chronologers hold the order as it stands. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) would read simply and there was, there being no indication of time in the original, and finds the phrase purposely indefinite. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) place it among the matters appended to the reign’s close. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) makes the silence the difficulty instead: of this famine we know nothing, and no such fact as the slaying of the Gibeonites appears in Saul’s life or anywhere else in Scripture.

Why the reckoning came so late, and fell on others, Ellicott answers nationally: Saul slew them not as the son of Kish but as king of Israel, involving all Israel in the violation of the national oath, so that until the evil were put away all Israel must suffer, and the lesson of the nation’s continued responsibility from age to age was greatly enhanced by the delay. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) will not have the question pressed, since God’s judgments often look a great way back and there is no statute of limitation to be pleaded against God’s demands. On what made the sin so great the three who treat it converge on the oath and divide on the motive. Henry holds that Saul acted under colour of zeal for Israel’s honour, that he might seem wiser than the judges before him, and perhaps meant it for an instance of royal prerogative, the power to disannul the most solemn leagues; it may be he designed this severity to atone for his clemency towards the Amalekites. What made it exceedingly sinful was that he not only shed innocent blood but therein violated the oath by which the nation was bound. Ellicott judges the zeal itself of the same ungodly character as much else in that reign, pride and self-will cloaked under a care for God’s honour. Wesley describes the method: he sought to cut them off with some colour of justice, aggravating their faults and oppressing them with excessive labours, intending by degrees to wear them out.

That they asked no money is read as principle, and the asking itself is questioned. Henry observes that money is no satisfaction for blood, that those over-value money and under-value life who sell their relations’ blood for corruptible things, and that the Gibeonites had a fair opportunity to demand discharge from their servitude and did not take it — though the covenant was broken on the other side it should not be broken on theirs. Ellicott notes that money compensation for blood was common among ancient nations but forbidden in the law of Israel, which these Gibeonites appear to have accepted, and that they asked no Israelite to suffer apart from Saul’s own connection with the crime. Clarke alone objects to the procedure: it is very strange that a choice of this kind should be left to such a people, and why was it not asked of God himself?
10:
Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) uses this scene to deny the whole transaction, and is alone in it. Did God require this sacrifice of Saul’s sons, he asks, probably all innocent of their father’s alleged crime? Was the requisition of the Gibeonites to be considered an oracle of God? Certainly not: God will not have man’s blood for sacrifice, no more than he will have swine’s blood, and the famine might have been removed by the sacrifices prescribed in the law and a general humiliation of the people. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) meets the difficulty from the other side, through the law requiring a hanged body to be buried the same day. He reports that one of the Jewish rabbin wished this passage expunged, that God’s name might be sanctified, thinking it dishonoured by his accepting a breach of his own law; but the case was extraordinary, and the very reason for the law is the reason for the exception — he that is left hanging is accursed, so ordinary malefactors must not be so used, and these must, being sacrificed not to the justice of the nation but for its crime.

Rizpah’s vigil draws unusual tenderness from all who touch it. John Gill (reformed) reads the sackcloth practically as well as mournfully, a token of grief and the fittest defence against the weather, heat by day and cold by night. Henry notes her restraint, that she might have cited the divine law to bear her out yet neither steals nor forces away the bodies, but patiently submits and pitches her tent near the gibbets. He then divides her conduct in two. In indulging her grief she did as mourners are too apt to do, to no good purpose, for when sorrow grows excessive we should study how to divert it rather than how to humour it. But in testifying her love she let the world know that her sons died for no sin of their own, not as stubborn and rebellious sons whose eye had despised to obey their mother, but for their father’s sin, so that her mind could not be alienated from them by their hard fate. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) gives that second judgment in almost the same words.

How long the watch lasted they do not agree. Clarke holds the rain must be the periodical autumn rains, which commence about October, and recoils at the arithmetic: is it possible that this broken-hearted woman watched these bodies, probably in the open air, more than five months? He rejects the alternative, that the rain was the mere breaking of the drought soon after the execution, as not agreeing with the way the account dates her watch from the beginning of harvest. Henry assumes the shorter reckoning without arguing it, supposing the rain came perhaps not many days after they were hung up.

That David buried them is traced to Rizpah by every voice. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) say that when her touching care for the dead was told him, he saw the bones of the whole fallen royal house buried in the family grave. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) adds the second motive, that David wished to show no enmity against the house of Saul. Gill will not guess whether the thing was told him out of good will or ill, but observes that it was not disagreeable to him, serving to move his pity and to show the execution had been obedience and not personal revenge. Henry adds the dignity of it, that royal dust should not be lost in the graves of the common people. Wesley has him hear of it with such approbation that he thought fit to imitate her piety, being provoked by her example to do what he had hitherto neglected, that the honour done the dead might comfort this disconsolate widow.
15:
Who actually killed the giant is left open by the grammar, and the voices divide. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) say flatly that Abishai came to the king’s help and slew him. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) reads it the other way and marks it as his own judgment: when Abishai had succoured him, giving him a cordial, it may be, or appearing as his second, it was David who smote the Philistine and killed him — which he grounds on the chapter’s own closing notice that David had a hand in slaying the giants. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) states the ambiguity rather than resolving it: the original leaves it doubtful whether Abishai is the subject of the verb or whether it should be simply he, referring to David, and the closing notice does seem to imply that one of the sons of the giant at least fell by David’s own hand.

The giant’s name is admitted to be strange, and the treatments differ in kind. Keil and Delitzsch take it as a genuine proper name rather than a man of Nob, probably meaning that his dwelling is on the height, a name he may have had from an inaccessible castle; and they trace him to the tribe-father of the Rephaim, of whom only a few families survived even in the time of Moses. Ellicott thinks rather that some error has crept into the text, grants that no proposed emendation is free from difficulty, and gives as the likeliest the Speaker’s Commentary’s, which reads they halted for the first element and, by a change of a single letter, at Gob for the second, yielding a text running David waxed faint, and they halted at Gob, and there was a man which was of the sons of the giant — a reading he supports from the next verses, which seem to presuppose an earlier battle at Gob. John Gill (reformed) asks only whether the phrase means Goliath’s own sons or the race in general.

That the king was old is what the passage turns on. Henry praises the going out: David, though old, desired no writ of ease from the public service but went in person, which shows he fought not for his own glory, being already loaded with glory and needing no more, but for the good of his kingdom. Then he marks the failure: David thought he could bear the fatigues of war as formerly, and his will was good, but he found himself deceived, for age had cut his hair, and after a little toil he waxed faint. The champion was soon aware of the advantage and thought to slay him, but God was not in his thoughts, and in that very day they all perished, for there is no strength, nor counsel, nor confidence against the Lord. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) notes that the fainting is recorded nowhere else, and that the parallel in Chronicles does not mention this war at all.

On the oath itself the readings are complementary. Keil and Delitzsch explain the title, that Jehovah was his light and had lighted his lamp and enlightened his darkness. Clarke takes the lamp as the emblem of direction and support, David being the light by which all Israel was guided and without whom the nation must be involved in darkness, and he cites a line of Homer using light in the same sense, of one who had failed to be a light to Patroclus and his companions. Henry calls him the guide and glory of Israel, says the oath was resolved in council to keep that light from ever again being put in hazard of being blown out, and draws the rule that the lives of those as valuable to their country as David was ought to be preserved with a double care, by themselves and by others.
18:
Here Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) gathers his objections into a twelve-point indictment of the chapter itself, and no other voice attempts the like. The three-year famine is spoken of nowhere else and was too remarkable to omit; Saul’s attempt on the Gibeonites is nowhere else mentioned and was such a breach of the national faith as could scarcely have failed to raise an insurrection; that seven innocent men should hang for an offending father seems inconsistent with justice and mercy; Rizpah’s months of watching are as related very improbable; and the long hanging was against an express law which God did not command a breach of. His conclusion is unguarded: it seems as if a Gibeonite has had a hand in the copies that have come down to us, or the first fourteen verses were inserted from a less authentic document, and till he gets further light he concludes that the whole chapter is not now what it would be from the pen of an inspired writer. He insists even so that the great foundation of God stands sure.

The verse that provokes him most makes Elhanan the slayer of Goliath, and all three textual voices work on it. Clarke calls it a most manifest corruption, since David and not Elhanan slew Goliath, and notes that our translators borrowed words from Chronicles to make the two agree; he accounts for it by supposing the word for weavers slipped from one line into the other and the Bethlehemite is a corruption of the giant’s name, which restores the Chronicles reading. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) reach the same mechanism and report the division among commentators, most holding the Chronicles text original and this one corrupt, others the reverse. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) agrees the word for weavers crept in from the line below, observes that the words the brother of are not in the Hebrew here but supplied from Chronicles, and preserves a curious Jewish tradition that this Elhanan was David himself, the Chaldee paraphrasing it as David the son of Jesse, the weaver of veils for the sanctuary, who was of Bethlehem, slew Goliath the Gittite.

Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) alone treats the four combats as a single lesson. The giants were probably the remains of the sons of Anak, who though long feared fell at last, and he notes of the last that having seen the others fall he defied Israel still. From this he draws three things: that it is folly for the strong man to glory in his strength, since David’s servants were no bigger than other men yet by divine assistance mastered one giant after another, God choosing by the weak things to confound the mighty; that the terror of the mighty in the land of the living commonly goes down slain to the pit; and that the most powerful enemies are often reserved for the last conflict, David having begun his glory with one giant and concluded it with four — for death is a Christian’s last enemy and a son of Anak, yet through him that triumphed for us we hope to be more than conquerors even over that enemy.

Two small questions remain. John Gill (reformed) will not have these born to Goliath, since one was his brother, but to some giant of Gath, and reports the Greek naming their family Repha, with Abarbinel taking Repha for a woman among the daughters of the giants and the Talmudists identifying her with Orpah. On the Jonathan who killed the last of them the two differ mildly: Ellicott makes him David’s nephew and probably the brother of the wily Jonadab, remarking that David’s family connections seem to have made up a clan of heroes, while Henry says he would have taken the two for one man but that Jonadab was noted for subtlety and this Jonathan for bravery.
